Brushed-metal windows in Mac OS X

A second Aqua window style with a brushed-aluminium texture, used for QuickTime Player, iTunes, the Finder, and Safari.

Source
Wikipedia: Aqua (user interface)
Creator
Apple
Made
First in QuickTime Player 4 (1999); widest use in Mac OS X Panther (2003); merged into one gray window style in Leopard (2007)
Style
Skeuomorphism (precursor; agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Metallic, cool, industrial
Evidence
No image was inspected. Based on Wikipedia, which cites Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines and Daring Fireball.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

“Brushed-metal windows had a thick frame with a metallic texture or dark-gray background and sunken buttons and inner frames.” “Apple recommended brushed-metal windows for applications that mimic real-world devices (such as iTunes) or are used to interface with such devices (such as iSync).” Wikipedia: Aqua).

“Brushed Metal had first appeared in QuickTime Player 4.” Panther used it more, “especially to the Finder and Safari web browser.” In Leopard, Aqua and brushed-metal windows “obtained the same metal-like, gray look.” Wikipedia: Aqua).

Wikipedia links the change to Apple’s industrial design: “In 2003 and 2004, Apple moved to the use of brushed aluminium … The design of Aqua changed accordingly.”

Why it belongs

Apple’s own rule tied the texture to device-like apps. That is the logic of the later style: the material says what kind of object the app is.

See the parent interface, Aqua.
